sub_skills.skill_name: Be specific in what you want
sub_skills.skill_content: When you ask an AI to do something, clear and exact words help it give the answer you want. State the goal, the format, and any limits up front. Say who the answer is for, how long it should be, and what to leave out. If numbers, dates, or sources matter, name them. For example, rather than “Explain World War II,” try “List three key events of World War II with dates and one short fact for each.” Being this precise cuts down on guesswork, avoids unwanted extra detail, and saves time by reducing follow-up questions.

rsc.title: AI Prompting Examples, Templates, and Tips For Educators
How to Ask AI for Anything: The Art of Prompting

sub_skills.skill_content: Provide additional context means giving the AI enough background facts, constraints, and goals so it can reply in the way you need. Start by naming the topic and the purpose of the answer. Add who the answer is for, the tone you want, and any limits such as length, format, or style. List key facts, data, or examples that matter to the task. This extra detail stops the model from guessing and keeps replies on target. Think of it like guiding a new teammate: share the details they need, but keep them short and clear.

rsc.title: What is Context in Prompt Engineering?
The Importance of Context for Reliable AI Systems

sub_skills.skill_content: Using relevant technical terms means including precise vocabulary from the domain of the task instead of describing things in vague, general language. A model trained on technical text responds better to prompts phrased the way experts in that field would phrase them. This reduces ambiguity and helps the model retrieve and apply the right knowledge for the task.

AI Agent Examples & Use Cases: Real Applications in 2025

sub_skills.skill_content: A clear way to guide an AI is to place one or two short samples inside your prompt. Show a small input and the exact output you expect. The AI studies these pairs and copies their pattern. Use plain words in the sample, keep the format steady, and label each part so the model knows which is which. If you need a list, show a list; if you need a table, include a small table. Good examples cut guesswork, reduce errors, and save you from writing long rules.

rsc.title: AI Agent Examples & Use Cases: Real Applications in 2025

sub_skills.skill_content: After you write a first prompt, treat it as a draft, not the final version. Run it with the AI, check the output, and note what is missing, wrong, or confusing. Change one thing at a time, such as adding an example, a limit on length, or a tone request. Test again and see if the result gets closer to what you want. Keep a record of each change and its effect, so you can learn patterns that work. Stop when the output is clear, correct, and repeatable. This loop of try, observe, adjust, and retry turns a rough prompt into a strong one.

When you give a task to an AI, make clear how long the answer should be and what shape it must take. Say “Write 120 words” or “Give the steps as a numbered list.” If you need a table, state the column names and order. If you want bullet points, mention that. Telling the AI to use plain text, JSON, or markdown stops guesswork and saves time. Clear limits on length keep the reply focused. A fixed format makes it easier for people or other software to read and use the result. Always put these rules near the start of your prompt so the AI sees them as important.

rsc.title: Mastering Prompt Engineering: Format, Length, and Audience

skills.skill_content: Chain of Thought (CoT) is a way for an AI agent to think out loud. Before giving its final answer, the agent writes short notes that show each step it takes. These notes can list facts, name sub-tasks, or do small bits of math. By seeing the steps, the agent stays organized and is less likely to make a mistake. People who read the answer can also check the logic and spot any weak points. The same written steps can be fed back into the agent so it can plan, reflect, or fix itself. Because it is easy to use and boosts trust, CoT is one of the most common designs for language-based agents today.

rsc.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
Evoking Chain of Thought Reasoning in LLMs - Prompting Guide

skills.skill_content: Tree-of-Thought is a way to organize an AI agent’s reasoning as a branching tree. At the root, the agent states the main problem. Each branch is a small idea, step, or guess that could lead to a solution. The agent expands the most promising branches, checks if they make sense, and prunes paths that look wrong or unhelpful. This setup helps the agent explore many possible answers while staying focused on the best ones. Because the agent can compare different branches side by side, it is less likely to get stuck on a bad line of thought. The result is more reliable and creative problem solving.

rsc.title: Tree of Thoughts (ToT) | Prompt Engineering Guide
The Revolutionary Approach of Tree-of-Thought Prompting in AI

sub_skills.skill_content: Web search lets an AI agent pull fresh facts, news, and examples from the internet while it is working. The agent turns a user request into search words, sends them to a search engine, and reads the list of results. It then follows the most promising links, grabs the page text, and picks out the parts that answer the task. This helps the agent handle topics that were not in its training data, update old knowledge, or double-check details. Web search covers almost any subject and is much faster than manual research, but the agent must watch for ads, bias, or wrong pages and cross-check sources to stay accurate.

A code execution or REPL tool lets an agent run code and see the actual result, rather than only generating code as text. This is useful for tasks like calculations, data processing, or verifying that generated code works before presenting it. Giving an agent this tool turns it from something that writes code into something that can test and correct its own output.

rsc.title: Building an AI Agent's Code Execution Environment

sub_skills.skill_content: Database queries let an AI agent fetch, add, change, or remove data stored in a database. The agent sends a request written in a query language, most often SQL. The database engine then looks through its tables and returns only the rows and columns that match the rules in the request. With this tool, the agent can answer questions that need up-to-date numbers, user records, or other stored facts. It can also write new entries or adjust old ones to keep the data current. Because queries work in real time and follow clear rules, they give the agent a reliable way to handle large sets of structured information.

API requests let an AI agent ask another service for data or for an action. The agent builds a short message that follows the service’s rules, sends it over the internet, and waits for a reply. For example, it can call a weather API to get today’s forecast or a payment API to charge a customer. Each request has a method like GET or POST, a URL, and often a small block of JSON with needed details. The service answers with another JSON block that the agent reads and uses. Because API requests are fast and clear, they are a common tool for connecting the agent to many other systems without extra work.

rsc.title: Introduction to APIs - MDN Web Docs
How APIs Power AI Agents: A Comprehensive Guide

sub_skills.skill_content: Email, Slack, and SMS are message channels an AI agent can use to act on tasks and share updates. The agent writes and sends emails to give detailed reports or collect files. It posts to Slack to chat with a team, answer questions, or trigger alerts inside a workspace. It sends SMS texts for quick notices such as reminders, confirmations, or warnings when a fast response is needed. By picking the right channel, the agent reaches users where they already communicate, makes sure important information arrives on time, and can even gather replies to keep a task moving forward.

File system access lets an AI agent read, create, change, or delete files and folders on a computer or server. With this power, the agent can open a text file to pull data, write a new report, save logs, or tidy up old files without human help. It can also move files between folders to keep things organized. This tool is useful for tasks such as data processing, report generation, and backup jobs. Strong safety checks are needed so the agent touches only the right files, avoids private data, and cannot harm the system by mistake.

skills.skill_content: A tool definition describes a function an agent can call, including its name, purpose, and the parameters it accepts, usually specified in a structured format like JSON schema. The language model reads this definition to decide when the tool is relevant and how to fill in its arguments. Clear, well documented tool definitions directly affect how reliably an agent chooses and uses the right tool.

rsc.title: Understanding the Agent Function in AI: Key Roles and Responsibilities

sub_skills.skill_content: MCP Hosts are computers or services that run the Model Context Protocol. They handle incoming calls, load the MCP manifest, check requests, and pass data between users, tools, and language models. Hosts may cache recent messages, track token usage, and add safety or billing checks before sending prompts to the model. They expose an API endpoint so apps can connect easily. You can run a host on your laptop for testing or deploy it on cloud platforms for scale. The host acts as the trusted bridge where agents, tools, and data meet.

rsc.title: AWS MCP Servers for Code Assistants

sub_skills.skill_content: The MCP Client is the part of an AI agent that talks to the language model API. It collects messages, files, and tool signals, packs them using the Model Context Protocol, and sends them to the model. When a reply comes back, it unpacks it, checks the format, and passes the result to other modules. It also tracks token usage, filters private data, retries failed calls, and logs important events for debugging.

An MCP server exposes a set of tools, data, or capabilities to any compatible client using the Model Context Protocol. It might, for example, provide access to a file system, a database, or a third party API. Because servers follow a shared protocol, they can be reused across different AI applications without custom integration work.

rsc.title: Security Holes in MCP Servers and How To Plug Them
Exploring File Uploads and Downloads in MCP
AWS MCP Servers for Code Assistants

skills.skill_content: Agent memory is the part of an AI agent that keeps track of what has already happened. It stores past user messages, facts the agent has learned, and its own previous steps. This helps the agent remember goals, user likes and dislikes, and important details across turns or sessions. Memory can be short-term, lasting only for one conversation, or long-term, lasting across many. With a good memory the agent avoids repeating questions, stays consistent, and plans better actions. Without it, the agent would forget everything each time and feel unfocused.

rsc.title: Storing and Retrieving Knowledge for Agents
Building Brain-Like Memory for AI Agents

skills.skill_content: Short-term memory refers to the immediate, transient information that an AI agent holds during a specific task or conversation. It is typically implemented by including recent interaction history, active goals, and relevant context directly within the model's prompt window. This data allows the agent to maintain coherence and follow the flow of a single session, though this information is usually cleared once the context limit is reached or the session ends.

rsc.title: Build Smarter AI Agents: Manage Short-term and Long-term Memory
Storing and Retrieving Knowledge for Agents
Building Brain-Like Memory for AI Agents

skills.skill_content: Agent memory often has two parts. Episodic memory is relevant to the context of the current conversation and may be lost after the conversation ends. Semantic memory is relevant to the broader knowledge of the agent and is persistent.

rsc.title: What Is AI Agent Memory? - IBM
Episodic Memory vs. Semantic Memory: The Key Differences

sub_skills.skill_content: Using RAG with a vector database means storing pieces of information as embeddings and retrieving the most relevant ones by similarity search when the agent needs context. This combination lets an agent access a large body of knowledge without keeping it all in the prompt, since only the relevant retrieved pieces get added to context. It is a common way to give agents access to long term or external memory.

rsc.title: Understanding Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Vector Databases
What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation, aka RAG?

sub_skills.skill_content: User profile storage is the part of an AI agent’s memory that holds stable facts about each user, such as name, age group, language, past choices, and long-term goals. The agent saves this data in a file or small database so it can load it each time the same user returns. By keeping the profile separate from short-term conversation logs, the agent can remember preferences without mixing them with temporary chat history. The profile is updated only when the user states a new lasting preference or when old information changes, which helps prevent drift or bloat.

sub_skills.skill_content: Summarization or compression reduces the size of stored or in context information by condensing it into a shorter form that keeps the key details. This is used when conversation history or retrieved data grows too large to fit within a context window. Compressing older information lets an agent retain the gist of past interactions without spending excessive tokens on the full detail.

Forgetting or aging strategies decide what stored information an agent should discard or deprioritize over time, since keeping everything indefinitely is neither practical nor useful. Common approaches include removing information after a set time, lowering its priority if it is not accessed, or replacing outdated details with newer ones. These strategies keep an agent's memory relevant and prevent it from being cluttered with stale or contradictory information.

skills.skill_content: Long term memory in an AI agent stores important information for future use, like a digital notebook. It saves facts, past events, user preferences, and learned skills so the agent can make smarter and more consistent decisions over time. Unlike short-term memory, this data survives across sessions. When a similar situation comes up, the agent can look back and use what it already knows. Long term memory usually lives in a database, file system, or vector store and may hold text, numbers, embeddings, or past conversation states. Good management of long-term memory is key for building agents that feel personalized and get better with experience.

skills.skill_content: A RAG agent combines retrieval augmented generation with the ability to take actions, retrieving relevant documents as part of its reasoning process rather than just as a one time context lookup before generating text. This lets it decide when retrieval is needed and query external knowledge sources multiple times during a task. It is commonly used for question answering over private or specialized document collections.

skills.skill_content: A planner executor architecture splits an agent into two roles: a planner that breaks a goal down into a sequence of steps, and an executor that carries out each step and reports back the result. This separation lets the planner focus on high level strategy while the executor handles the details of each individual action. It can make an agent's behavior easier to reason about and debug compared to a single combined loop.

skills.skill_content: Building an AI agent from scratch means writing every part of the system yourself, without ready-made libraries. You define how the agent senses inputs, stores memory, makes decisions, and learns over time. First, you pick a clear goal, like solving puzzles or chatting. Then you code the inputs (keyboard, mouse, text), decision logic (rules or neural networks), and memory (saving facts from past events). Testing is critical: you run the agent, watch its actions, debug, and improve. Though it takes longer, this approach gives deep understanding and full control over how the agent works and evolves.

sub_skills.skill_content: LangSmith is a platform for debugging, testing, and monitoring LLM applications, including agents, by tracing each step of a run and logging inputs, outputs, and intermediate reasoning. It also supports building evaluation datasets and running automated tests against them to measure quality over time, alongside dashboards for tracking cost and latency in production. Built by the LangChain team, it is commonly paired with LangChain and LangGraph applications but can be used independently.

sub_skills.skill_content: DeepEval is an open-source tool that helps you test and score the answers your AI agent gives. You write small test cases that show an input and the reply you hope to get, or a rule the reply must follow. DeepEval runs the agent, checks the reply with built-in measures such as similarity, accuracy, or safety, and then marks each test as pass or fail. You can add your own checks, store tests in code or YAML files, and run them in a CI pipeline so every new model or prompt version gets the same quick audit. The fast feedback makes it easy to spot errors, cut down on hallucinations, and compare different models before you ship.

rsc.title: DeepEval - The Open-Source LLM Evaluation Framework

sub_skills.skill_content: Ragas is an evaluation framework focused specifically on retrieval augmented generation pipelines, measuring things like the relevance of retrieved documents and the faithfulness of generated answers to that retrieved content. It provides a standard set of metrics tailored to RAG systems rather than general purpose LLM evaluation. This makes it useful for diagnosing whether errors come from the retrieval step or the generation step.

skills.skill_content: LLM native function calling is a capability built directly into a model's API that lets it output a structured call to a predefined function, including the function name and arguments, instead of freeform text. The application executes the actual function and returns the result to the model to continue the conversation. This standardizes how models request actions, removing the need to parse tool calls out of plain text output.

sub_skills.skill_content: OpenAI's function calling lets a model choose from a set of functions defined in the API request and return a structured call with the function name and arguments as JSON. The calling application executes the function and sends the result back for the model to use in its next response. It is one of the earliest and most widely adopted implementations of native tool calling.

sub_skills.skill_content: The OpenAI Assistants API is a higher level interface for building agents that manages conversation threads, tool calls, and file based context on OpenAI's servers, rather than requiring the developer to track state manually. It handles things like persisting conversation history and running tools like code execution or file search. This reduces the amount of infrastructure a developer needs to build to get a working agent.

sub_skills.skill_content: Gemini function calling is Google's implementation of native tool calling, letting a Gemini model select from provided function definitions and return a structured call with arguments. The application runs the corresponding function and returns the output to continue the interaction. It follows the same general pattern as other providers' function calling, with its own specific request and response format.

sub_skills.skill_content: Anthropic tool use is Claude's implementation of native function calling, where the model can choose to call a defined tool with structured arguments as part of its response. The calling application executes the tool and returns the result, which Claude can use to continue reasoning or produce a final answer. It supports patterns like parallel tool calls and forcing a specific tool to be used when needed.

LangChain is a framework designed to simplify the creation of applications using large language models (LLMs). It provides tools and abstractions to connect LLMs to various data sources, create chains of calls to LLMs or other utilities, and build agents that can interact with their environment. Essentially, it helps developers structure, chain, and orchestrate different AI components to build more complex and capable AI applications.

sub_skills.skill_content: LangGraph is a Python library designed to help developers create robust and stateful conversational AI applications, often referred to as AI Agents. It allows you to structure complex agent workflows by defining states (data held throughout the conversation) and edges (transitions between states based on agent decisions or external events), creating a graph-like representation of the agent's reasoning process. This makes it easier to manage the flow of conversations and build more reliable and explainable AI agents.

sub_skills.skill_content: Haystack is an open source framework for building search and question answering pipelines, including retrieval augmented generation and agent based applications. It provides modular components for document retrieval, ranking, and generation that can be combined into custom pipelines. It is often used in production search and NLP applications that need a flexible, composable architecture.

LlamaIndex is a framework focused on connecting language models to external data, providing tools for ingesting, indexing, and querying documents for retrieval augmented generation. It handles tasks like chunking documents, generating embeddings, and building indexes that support efficient retrieval. It is commonly used as the data layer underneath a RAG based agent.

CrewAI is an open-source Python framework for creating teams of AI agents, called a crew. Each agent is assigned a name, role, and set of tools, and the system manages planning, communication, and execution between them. To use it, install the package, define agents in code, connect them with a `Crew` object, and assign a mission prompt. CrewAI interacts with an LLM like GPT-4 or Claude, passes messages, runs tools, and returns a final output. You can also add web search, custom functions, or memory stores. Logs are built-in to help debug and optimize workflows.

sub_skills.skill_content: AutoGen is a framework from Microsoft for building applications with multiple agents that communicate with each other to solve tasks. It defines agents with specific roles and lets them exchange messages, delegate subtasks, and collaborate toward a shared goal. It is commonly used for research and applications that benefit from multiple specialized agents working together.

Smol Depot is an open-source kit that lets you bundle all the parts of a small AI agent in one place. You keep prompts, settings, and code files together in a single folder, then point the Depot tool at that folder to spin the agent up. The tool handles tasks such as loading models, saving chat history, and calling outside APIs, so you do not have to write that glue code yourself. A simple command can copy a starter template, letting you focus on the logic and prompts that make your agent special. Because everything lives in plain files, you can track changes with Git and share the agent like any other project.

sub_skills.skill_content: Agno is a Python framework designed to streamline the process of building AI agents. It offers tools and abstractions that simplify tasks such as agent planning, tool use, and memory management, making it easier to create sophisticated and functional AI agents without managing low-level implementation details. It emphasizes modularity and composability, enabling developers to easily integrate different components and customize agent behavior.

sub_skills.skill_content: Structured logging and tracing record an agent's execution in a consistent, machine readable format, capturing details like which tool was called, what arguments were used, and how long each step took. Unlike plain text logs, structured data can be filtered, searched, and analyzed programmatically. Tracing connects these individual log entries into a full picture of a single run, which is essential for debugging complex, multi step agent behavior.

sub_skills.skill_content: LangSmith is a web tool that helps you see and fix what your AI agents are doing. It records each call that the agent makes to a language model, the input it used, and the answer it got back. You can replay any step, compare different prompts, measure cost, speed, and error rates, and tag runs for easy search. It also lets you store test sets and run quick checks so you know if new code makes the agent worse. By showing clear traces and charts, LangSmith makes it easier to debug, improve, and trust AI systems built with LangChain or other frameworks.

sub_skills.skill_content: Helicone is an open-source tool that helps you watch and understand how your AI agents talk to large language models. You send your model calls through Helicone’s proxy, and it records each request and response without changing the result. A clear web dashboard then shows logs, latency, token counts, error rates, and cost for every call. You can filter, search, and trace a single user journey, which makes it easy to spot slow prompts or rising costs. Helicone also lets you set alerts and share traces with your team, so problems get fixed fast and future changes are safer.

Langfuse is an open source observability and analytics platform for LLM applications, providing tracing, evaluation, and prompt management features. It captures detailed traces of agent runs, including nested tool calls, and lets teams analyze performance and quality over time. It can be self hosted, which appeals to teams with strict data privacy requirements.

sub_skills.skill_content: OpenLLMetry is an open source observability standard that extends OpenTelemetry, a widely used tracing framework, to cover LLM specific data like prompts, completions, and token usage. It lets teams instrument their LLM applications using familiar observability tooling rather than a separate, proprietary system. This makes it easier to integrate LLM monitoring into existing infrastructure that already uses OpenTelemetry.

skills.skill_content: Tool sandboxing keeps the AI agent inside a safe zone where it can only run approved actions and cannot touch the wider system. Permissioning sets clear rules that say which files, networks, or commands the agent may use. Together they stop errors, leaks, or abuse by limiting what the agent can reach and do. Developers grant the smallest set of rights, watch activity, and block anything outside the plan. If the agent needs new access, it must ask and get a fresh permit. This simple fence protects user data, reduces harm, and builds trust in the agent’s work.

skills.skill_content: AI agents often process text, images, and logs that include personal data like names, phone numbers, or addresses. Leaks can cause fraud, stalking, or other harm, so laws like GDPR and CCPA require strict protections. A key method is PII redaction: scanning inputs and outputs to find and mask any personal details before storage or sharing. Redaction uses pattern rules, machine learning, or both. Teams should also keep audit logs, enforce access controls, and test their redaction flows often to prevent leaks.

skills.skill_content: Bias and toxicity guardrails are checks put in place to detect and block outputs that are discriminatory, offensive, or otherwise harmful before they reach a user. These can be implemented through classifier models, keyword filters, or the underlying model's own safety training. They are important for agents that generate open ended content or interact directly with end users.

sub_skills.skill_content: To judge how well an AI agent works, you need clear numbers. Track accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score to measure correctness. For ranking tasks, use metrics like mean average precision or ROC-AUC. If users interact with the agent, monitor response time, latency, and failure rates. Safety metrics count toxic or biased outputs, while robustness tests check how the agent handles messy or tricky inputs. Resource metrics—memory, CPU, and energy—show if it can scale. Pick the metrics that match your goal, compare against a baseline, and track trends across versions.

sub_skills.skill_content: Unit testing checks that each tool an AI agent uses works as expected when it stands alone. You write small tests that feed the tool clear input and then compare its output to a known correct answer. If the tool is a function that parses dates, you test many date strings and see if the function gives the right results. Good tests cover normal cases, edge cases, and error cases. Run the tests every time you change the code. When a test fails, fix the tool before moving on. This habit keeps bugs from spreading into larger agent workflows and makes later debugging faster.

sub_skills.skill_content: Integration testing for flows checks that an agent behaves correctly across a full multi step task, not just that individual tools work on their own. It verifies that the agent chooses the right tools in the right order and handles the combined behavior of reasoning, acting, and observing correctly. This catches issues that only show up when components interact, which unit tests on individual pieces would miss.

sub_skills.skill_content: Human-in-the-loop evaluation checks an AI agent by letting real people judge its output and behavior. Instead of trusting only automated scores, testers invite users, domain experts, or crowd workers to watch tasks, label answers, flag errors, and rate clarity, fairness, or safety. Their feedback shows problems that numbers alone miss, such as hidden bias, confusing language, or actions that feel wrong to a person. Teams study these notes, adjust the model, and run another round, repeating until the agent meets quality and trust goals. Mixing human judgment with data leads to a system that is more accurate, useful, and safe for everyday use.

skills.skill_content: Safety + Red Team Testing is the practice of checking an AI agent for harmful or risky behavior before and after release. Safety work sets rules, guardrails, and alarms so the agent follows laws, keeps data private, and treats people fairly. Red team testing sends skilled testers to act like attackers or troublemakers. They type tricky prompts, try to leak private data, force biased outputs, or cause the agent to give dangerous advice. Every weakness they find is logged and fixed by adding filters, better training data, stronger limits, or live monitoring. Running these tests often lowers the chance of real-world harm and builds trust with users and regulators.

sub_skills.skill_content: A Local Desktop deployment means running the MCP server directly on your own computer instead of a remote cloud or server. You install the MCP software, needed runtimes, and model files onto your desktop or laptop. The server then listens on a local address like `127.0.0.1:8000`, accessible only from the same machine unless you open ports manually. This setup is great for fast tests, personal demos, or private experiments since you keep full control and avoid cloud costs. However, it's limited by your hardware's speed and memory, and others cannot access it without tunneling tools like ngrok or local port forwarding.

sub_skills.skill_content: Remote or cloud deployment places the MCP server on a cloud provider instead of a local machine. You package the server as a container or virtual machine, choose a service like AWS, Azure, or GCP, and give it compute, storage, and a public HTTPS address. A load balancer spreads traffic, while auto-scaling adds or removes copies of the server as demand changes. You secure the endpoint with TLS, API keys, and firewalls, and you send logs and metrics to the provider’s monitoring tools. This setup lets the server handle many users, updates are easier, and you avoid local hardware limits, though you must watch costs and protect sensitive data.

skills.skill_content: Fine-tuning and prompt engineering are two ways to get better outputs from a language model. Fine-tuning means training an existing model further with your own examples so it adapts to specific tasks. It needs extra data, computing power, and time but creates deeply specialized models. Prompt engineering, in contrast, leaves the model unchanged and focuses on crafting better instructions or examples in the prompt itself. It is faster, cheaper, and safer when no custom data is available. Fine-tuning suits deep domain needs; prompt engineering fits quick control and prototyping.

skills.skill_content: Prompt engineering is the skill of writing clear questions or instructions so that an AI system gives the answer you want. It means choosing the right words, adding enough detail, and giving examples when needed. A good prompt tells the AI what role to play, what style to use, and what facts to include or avoid. By testing and refining the prompt, you can improve the quality, accuracy, and usefulness of the AI’s response. In short, prompt engineering is guiding the AI with well-designed text so it can help you better.

skills.skill_content: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that defines how AI applications connect to external tools, data sources, and services in a consistent way. Instead of building a custom integration for every tool an agent needs, MCP provides a common interface that any compliant client and server can use to communicate. This makes it easier to plug new capabilities into an agent without writing bespoke connection code each time.

Start by picking a language and web framework, then create REST endpoints like `/messages`, `/state`, and `/health`. Each endpoint exchanges JSON following the MCP schema. Store session logs with a session ID, role, and timestamp using a database or in-memory store. Add token-based authentication and filters so agents can fetch only what they need. Set limits on message size and request rates to avoid overload. Finally, write unit tests, add monitoring, and run load tests to ensure stability.

skills.skill_content: A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) agent is made of small parts called nodes that form a one-way graph with no loops. Each node does a task and passes its result to the next. Because there are no cycles, data always moves forward, making workflows easy to follow and debug. Independent nodes can run in parallel, speeding up tasks. If a node fails, you can trace and fix that part without touching the rest. DAG agents are ideal for jobs like data cleaning, multi-step reasoning, or workflows where backtracking isn’t needed.

sub_skills.skill_content: Multi-agent systems involve multiple autonomous agents that interact with each other to achieve individual or collective goals. These agents can collaborate, compete, or coordinate their actions within a shared environment. The interactions between these agents can lead to emergent behaviors and solutions that are more complex and sophisticated than what a single agent could achieve on its own.

sub_skills.skill_content: Self-critique agents are a type of AI agent designed to evaluate and improve their own performance. They work by generating outputs, then analyzing those outputs to identify weaknesses or errors. Based on this self-analysis, the agent refines its approach and attempts to produce better results in subsequent iterations. This cycle of generation, critique, and refinement allows the agent to learn and adapt over time, improving its ability to solve problems or complete tasks effectively.

skills.skill_content: Prompt injection, also called a jailbreak, is a trick that makes an AI system break its own rules. An attacker hides special words or symbols inside normal-looking text. When the AI reads this text, it follows the hidden instructions instead of its safety rules. The attacker might force the AI to reveal private data, produce harmful content, or give wrong advice. This risk grows when the AI talks to other software or pulls text from the internet, because harmful prompts can slip in without warning. Good defenses include cleaning user input, setting strong guardrails inside the model, checking outputs for policy breaks, and keeping humans in the loop for high-risk tasks.

skills.skill_content: Prompt engineering is the practice of writing inputs that get useful, reliable outputs from a large language model. It involves clear instructions, examples, output formats and reasoning techniques such as chain of thought. Context engineering widens the view to everything the model sees: instructions, retrieved documents, tool definitions, memory and conversation history. Together they decide how well an LLM-based application performs, from a simple assistant to an agent.

sub_skills.skill_content: Prompt engineering focuses on the wording and structure of the instructions you send to a model. Context engineering decides what information goes into the model's context window at each step, including documents, tool results, memory and history. The prompt is one part of the context. For a single chat request the prompt matters most, while for agents and RAG applications the quality of the surrounding context usually decides the result.

skills.skill_content: An LLM generates text by predicting the next token from all the tokens before it, then repeating the process. Base models are trained on raw text and simply continue it, while instruct models get extra training to follow instructions and hold conversations. Most models you use through chat apps and APIs are instruct models. Knowing this explains why the wording, examples and context in a prompt change the output.

sub_skills.skill_content: Reasoning models spend extra tokens thinking through a problem before they give a final answer. This makes them stronger at math, logic, coding and multi-step planning, but slower and more expensive than standard models. They need different prompting: clear goals work better than step-by-step instructions, since they already plan their own steps.

sub_skills.skill_content: Closed models, such as GPT, Claude and Gemini, are used through a provider's API and their weights are not public. Open-weights models, such as Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek and Mistral, can be downloaded, self-hosted and fine-tuned. Closed models usually lead on capability and are simple to start with. Open models give more control over cost, privacy and customization.

sub_skills.skill_content: Models come in different sizes, from small and fast ones to large frontier models. Larger models are usually more capable but cost more per token and respond more slowly. Many applications use a small model for simple tasks and a large one only for hard requests. Pricing is normally charged per input and output token, so prompt length affects the bill.

sub_skills.skill_content: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next token. From this one skill it can write, summarize, translate, answer questions and generate code. It produces its output one token at a time, based on the text it has been given.

Tokens are the pieces of text a model reads and writes, usually word fragments a few characters long. A word can be one token or several, and in English a token averages roughly three quarters of a word. Pricing, speed and context limits are all measured in tokens.

sub_skills.skill_content: The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can process in one request. It includes the prompt, the conversation history, any retrieved material and the model's own reply. Text beyond the limit has to be cut or left out. Larger windows allow more material, although quality can drop as they fill up.

sub_skills.skill_content: Fine-tuning trains a model further on your own examples to change its behavior, while prompt engineering changes only the input. Prompting is faster, cheaper and easy to iterate on, so it is usually the first thing to try. Fine-tuning makes sense when you need a consistent style or format at scale, or a specialized task that prompts cannot reach.

sub_skills.skill_content: RAG retrieves relevant documents and adds them to the prompt. Dynamic filters narrow the search with metadata such as date, source, user or document type, so the results are relevant to the request. Good retrieval depends on chunking, embeddings and often a reranking step. Retrieving less but more relevant material usually beats loading everything.

sub_skills.skill_content: Embeddings are lists of numbers that represent the meaning of a piece of text, so texts with similar meaning end up close together. Systems use them for semantic search: embed the documents and the query, then return the nearest matches. RAG pipelines depend on them to find relevant content.

sub_skills.skill_content: An agent is a system where an LLM decides its own next steps in a loop. It calls tools, reads the results and continues until the goal is reached. This differs from a fixed workflow, where the steps are decided in advance by the developer. Coding assistants and research assistants are common examples.

sub_skills.skill_content: A hallucination is when a model produces false or unsupported information in a confident tone. It happens because models generate likely text and do not check facts. Grounding answers in provided sources, asking for citations and verifying important outputs all reduce it.

sub_skills.skill_content: Chain of thought prompting asks the model to write out its reasoning steps before giving the final answer, for example by adding "think step by step" or by showing worked examples. It improves results on math, logic and multi-step problems. On reasoning models it is usually unnecessary, because they already think before answering.

sub_skills.skill_content: Tree of thoughts lets a model explore several reasoning paths, evaluate them and go back when one fails, instead of following a single chain. It suits planning and puzzle problems where the first idea is often wrong. It needs many model calls per task, so it is mostly used in research and special cases.

sub_skills.skill_content: Self-evaluation asks a model to review its own output against criteria and then fix problems. A typical pattern is draft, critique, revise. It can catch obvious errors and improve quality, but models are often overconfident about their own mistakes. Tests, sources and other external checks are more reliable when they are available.

rsc.title: The definitive guide to LLM evaluations

sub_skills.skill_content: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources. A tool is exposed once as an MCP server and can then be used by any client that supports the protocol, instead of writing a custom integration for each app. Servers can provide tools, resources and prompt templates.

rsc.title: MCP Explained: How Modern AI Agents Connect to the Real World - Towards Data Science
What is MCP? Integrate AI Agents with Databases & APIs

sub_skills.skill_content: Effort levels control how much a reasoning model thinks before it answers. Providers expose this as a level such as low, medium or high, or as a token budget for thinking, and the names differ between them. More effort improves results on hard problems but increases cost and latency. For simple tasks a low setting is usually enough.

rsc.title: Choosing the right reasoning level for LLM tasks
Anthropic Just Revealed Which Effort Level to Use

sub_skills.skill_content: Spec-driven prompts are structured inputs that rely on predefined schemas, such as JSON, XML, or YAML, to dictate the format and constraints of an AI's output. By providing a formal "specification" or template, you ensure that the model follows specific structural requirements, data types, and field naming conventions. This approach reduces ambiguity and ensures the generated content is machine-readable and ready for integration into larger software systems or automated workflows.

rsc.title: Full Course: Spec-Driven Development with Coding Agents
Spec-Driven Development: AI Assisted Coding Explained

sub_skills.skill_content: Prompt chaining splits a large task into a sequence of smaller prompts, where the output of one step becomes the input of the next. Each step is simpler, easier to test and easier to fix. A typical chain is extract, then analyze, then write. You can also add a check between steps to stop errors from carrying forward.

rsc.title: Chain complex prompts for stronger performance - Anthropic
Prompt Engineering Course Part 3 - Prompt Chaining

sub_skills.skill_content: Classification and routing use a first model call to decide what a request is, then send it to the right prompt, model or tool. The prompt lists the options with clear descriptions, keeps them from overlapping and includes an "other" choice for unclear input. Code then reads the label and acts on it. Examples include support ticket triage and sending easy questions to a smaller model.

Tool calling, also called function calling, lets a model request that your code run a function with specific arguments. You describe each tool with a name, a purpose and a JSON Schema for its inputs. The model replies with a tool request, your code executes it and returns the result, and the model uses it in its answer. Clear tool names and descriptions strongly affect how well the model picks the right one.

rsc.title: Function Calling vs. Tool Calling in LLMs: What’s the Difference?
What is Tool Calling? Connecting LLMs to Your Data
LLM Function Calling - AI Tools Deep Dive

skills.skill_content: The context is everything the model sees in one request. It usually includes the system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved documents, memory, the conversation history and the latest user message. Each part uses tokens from the same window. Knowing what is in the context helps you find why a model behaves a certain way.

rsc.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents - Anthropic
Context engineering explained: What every AI developer should know

sub_skills.skill_content: Context sources are the places where information in the context comes from. Common ones are user input, documents, databases, APIs, tool results, previous conversations and stored memory. Each source differs in reliability, freshness and cost, so deciding which ones to use and when is a core part of context engineering.

rsc.title: The Context Layer for AI: What Enterprises Get Wrong - DataHub
Most devs don't understand how context windows work

sub_skills.skill_content: Context failure modes are common ways that context causes bad output. Poisoning is when a wrong fact enters the context and keeps being reused. Distraction is when too much detail pulls the model away from the task. Confusion is when irrelevant material misleads it, and clash is when parts of the context contradict each other. Each one has a different fix.

rsc.title: How Long Contexts Fail - Drew Breunig
The 4 Failure Modes of Agent Context in Production
Context Engineering for AI Agents: 4 Failure Modes to Avoid

sub_skills.skill_content: Grounding means tying the model's answer to supplied sources. The prompt tells the model to answer only from the provided text, to say when the answer is not there and to quote or cite the passages it used. It is one of the simplest ways to reduce hallucinations, and it is the base of most RAG applications.

rsc.title: What Is Agentic Context Grounding? The Pattern Behind Claude Design and Vertical AI Apps
Context Grounding, RAG Strategies and Escalations-Giving Your Agent the Right Knowledge at the Right Time

skills.skill_content: Managing context means choosing what goes into the context window, in what order, and what to remove as a task goes on. The goal is to give the model what it needs for the current step and nothing more. Techniques include retrieval, memory, compaction, isolation and caching.

rsc.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents - Anthropic
Context Engineering as Your Competitive Edge

sub_skills.skill_content: State is the information a system tracks within one session, such as the current task and recent steps. Memory is what it keeps across sessions, such as user preferences or past decisions. Models do not remember anything by default, so both have to be stored outside the model and added back into the context when needed.

rsc.title: A Practical Guide to Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents
Memory Management in AI Agents - LangChain

The Four Types of Memory Every AI Agent Needs

sub_skills.skill_content: CLAUDE . md and AGENTS . md are markdown files kept in a project that coding agents read at the start of each session. They hold standing instructions such as build and test commands, code conventions and rules for the project. AGENTS . md is an open format used by several tools, and CLAUDE . md is the file Claude Code reads. Short, specific instructions work better than long ones.

rsc.title: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files: how to write and share them

sub_skills.skill_content: Context compaction shortens the context when it grows too long. The usual method is to summarize older conversation turns or tool results and keep only the important facts, decisions and open tasks. Some systems also clear old tool outputs. It frees space and cuts cost, but a bad summary can lose details the model needs later.

rsc.title: Context compaction for AI agents: a complete guide

What Do You Do When the Context Is Almost Full? How Does Context Compaction Work?

sub_skills.skill_content: Context rot is the drop in output quality as the context gets longer, even when it is within the window limit. Models can miss or misuse information buried in the middle of long inputs, and irrelevant text adds noise. In practice, it is better to keep context short and relevant than to fill the window.

rsc.title: Coding Agents Don't Need Bigger Context Windows - Towards Data Science
Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance

sub_skills.skill_content: Prompt injection is an attack where text in the input makes the model ignore its original instructions. It can be typed directly by a user, or hidden in content the model reads, such as a web page, an email or a document. It is hard to fully prevent, so defenses include separating trusted from untrusted content, limiting what the model can do and checking outputs.

rsc.title: Visit the Dedicated AI Red Teaming Roadmap

What Is a Prompt Injection Attack?

sub_skills.skill_content: A jailbreak is a prompt that gets a model to break its own safety rules and produce content it would normally refuse. Common methods include role-play scenarios, encoded text and long multi-turn pressure. Providers train against known jailbreaks, but new ones keep appearing, so applications should not rely on the model's refusals alone.

rsc.title: Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections - Anthropic

I Jailbroke My AI Coding Agent… It Actually Worked! 😳

sub_skills.skill_content: Output validation checks a model's response before it is shown to a user or passed to another system. Checks include validating JSON against a schema, filtering unsafe or off-topic content, and testing values against business rules. If a check fails, the system can retry, repair the output or send it to a person.

rsc.title: LLM output validation: 5 patterns that actually work in production
LLM Ops Architecture: Implementing Output Validation and Structured AI Responses

sub_skills.skill_content: Context security protects the information that goes into the context window. It deals with untrusted retrieved content, poisoned documents, and secrets or personal data that should not be exposed in a prompt or reply. The main practice is keeping trusted instructions separate from untrusted content and limiting what sensitive data enters the context at all.

rsc.title: Context Engineering Is Security Engineering. RSA 2026 Made the Case. - Zenity

sub_skills.skill_content: Agent and tool security limits what an agent can do if it is misled or makes a mistake. Practices include giving each tool the least permissions it needs, running code in a sandbox, requiring human approval for risky actions such as deleting data or sending money, and treating tool results as untrusted input. Tool outputs can carry injected instructions.

rsc.title: What Is LLM (Large Language Model) Security? | Starter Guide
Human in the Loop - Cloudflare Agents

sub_skills.skill_content: Prompt caching lets a provider reuse the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix between requests. It lowers cost and latency when the beginning of the prompt stays the same, such as the system prompt, tool definitions and reference documents. To benefit, put stable content first and changing content, such as the user's message, last.

rsc.title: What is Prompt Caching? Optimize LLM Latency with AI Transformers

sub_skills.skill_content: Context budgeting is deciding how many tokens each part of the context gets. System prompt, tools, retrieved documents, history and the model's reply all compete for the same window and add to cost and latency. A budget forces choices about what to keep, trim or retrieve on demand, and it helps keep quality steady in long-running tasks.

rsc.title: LLM Cost Optimization: 5 Levers That Cut API Spend 70-85% - Morph
The LLM Inference Trilemma: Throughput, Latency, Cost - DigitalOcean
Context Budget Allocation: Spending Every Token Wisely¶

skills.skill_content: A prompt is the input you give a model to get a response. It usually combines an instruction, optional background or data, examples and a description of the output format you want. Clearer and more specific prompts produce more predictable results.

sub_skills.skill_content: Delimiters are markers such as triple backticks, quotes or headings that separate one part of a prompt from another. XML tags like `<document>` and `<instructions>` do the same job and give each part a name you can refer to. They help the model distinguish instructions from data, and they make it harder for text inside the data to be mistaken for a command.

rsc.title: Use XML tags to structure your prompts - Anthropic
Delimiters and Separators in Prompts (Why They Matter)
Mastering XML Tags for Clarity, Precision, and Security in LLMs

sub_skills.skill_content: A prompt template is a prompt with placeholders, such as `{{customer_name}}`, that your code fills in at run time. It keeps the fixed instructions separate from the changing input, so the same prompt can be reused and tested. Templates also make versioning and evaluation easier, since only the variables change between runs.

rsc.title: Prompt Templates: The Secret Sauce for Smarter AI Prompts 🚀

skills.skill_content: Prompt structure is how you organize the parts of a prompt so the model can tell them apart. A common layout puts the role or task first, then the context or data, then the output requirements. Separating sections clearly reduces confusion, especially when the prompt contains user-supplied text.

rsc.title: Prompt Structure and Key Parts - LearnPrompting
Google's 9 Hour AI Prompt Engineering Course In 20 Minutes

skills.skill_content: Prompting approaches are the basic ways of shaping a request to a model. They differ in how many examples you give and where the instructions and background sit. The most common are zero-shot, few-shot, system, role and contextual prompting. Most real prompts combine several of them.

sub_skills.skill_content: Zero-shot prompting means asking the model to do a task with no examples, relying only on the instruction. It works well for common tasks such as summarizing, translating or answering simple questions. It is the usual starting point, and you add examples when the output is not what you want.

rsc.title: Zero-shot, One-shot and Few-shot Prompting Explained

sub_skills.skill_content: One-shot and few-shot prompting include one or several worked examples in the prompt before the real input. The model copies the pattern, which helps with output format, tone and unusual tasks. Examples should be consistent and cover varied cases, because the model tends to imitate them closely.

rsc.title: What is few shot prompting? - IBM
Zero-shot, One-shot and Few-shot Prompting Explained

sub_skills.skill_content: A system prompt is a set of instructions given before the conversation that sets the model's behavior, rules and output format. It usually holds the role, constraints, tone and background for the task. Instructions in it normally take priority over user messages, although this is not a guarantee against conflicting or malicious input.

rsc.title: User prompts vs. system prompts: What's the difference? - Regie.ai

skills.skill_content: Reasoning techniques are prompting methods that help a model work through problems step by step or check its own answers. Some change how the model reasons, such as chain of thought, while others improve reliability by comparing or reviewing several outputs. Reasoning models do much of this internally, so these techniques matter most for standard models.

rsc.title: What Are Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)? Smarter AI Beyond LLMs

skills.skill_content: Tools let a model act beyond generating text, for example by searching, querying a database or running code. Agents use tools in a loop and decide their own steps. Prompting for them means describing tools clearly, setting limits and keeping the context focused. Simpler fixed workflows are often more reliable than a full agent.

rsc.title: What is Tool Calling? Connecting LLMs to Your Data

skills.skill_content: Controlling outputs means shaping the format, length, style and variability of a model's response. Some controls are written in the prompt, such as asking for JSON. Others are API settings, such as maximum tokens or temperature. Applications that read the output with code need these controls to get consistent results.

rsc.title: Mastering Prompt Engineering: Format, Length, and Audience - Techlasi

sub_skills.skill_content: Structured outputs are responses in a fixed format such as JSON, XML or a table, so code can read them reliably. You can request them in the prompt by describing the fields and showing an example. This works most of the time but is not guaranteed, so the output should still be validated before use.

rsc.title: Generating Structured Outputs from LLMs - Towards Data Science

sub_skills.skill_content: Output limits control how much a model writes and where it stops. They keep responses short enough for your use case and keep cost and latency down. The main tools are a maximum token count, stop sequences and, for reasoning models, an effort setting.

rsc.title: General Tips for Designing Prompts - DAIR.AI

sub_skills.skill_content: Sampling parameters control how a model picks the next token from its probability distribution. They set how random or repetitive the output is. The main ones are temperature, top-K, top-P and repetition controls. Some newer models fix or limit these settings, so check what your model allows.

rsc.title: LLM Parameters Explained: A Practical Guide with Examples - LearnPrompting
Temperature vs Top-P vs Top-K (and Models That Ignore Them)

skills.skill_content: Multimodal inputs let a model work with images, PDFs, audio and sometimes video, as well as text. Prompts should say what to look at and what to extract, for example "list the line items and totals from this invoice." Check results on small or low-quality details, since models can misread them.

rsc.title: How to Write Multimodal Prompts for Images, Video, Audio, and Files
What is Multimodal AI? How LLMs Process Text, Images, and More

skills.skill_content: Prompt evaluation is measuring how well a prompt performs on a set of test cases. Instead of judging a few outputs by eye, you run the prompt on many inputs and score the results. It shows whether a change really helps and where the prompt fails.

rsc.title: LLM evaluation: a beginner's guide - Evidently AI
Define success criteria and build evaluations - Anthropic
What is prompt evaluation? How to test prompts with metrics and judges
Welcome to the LLM evaluation course

sub_skills.skill_content: An eval set is a collection of test inputs, often with expected outputs or scoring criteria. Good sets include typical cases, edge cases and past failures. They start small, with a few dozen examples, and grow as new problems appear. They are the base for comparing prompts and models.

rsc.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations - Anthropic
Demystifying evals for AI agents - Anthropic
AI Evaluation Design Guide: Building Evals That Actually Measure What Matters
How to Systematically Setup LLM Evals (Metrics, Unit Tests, LLM-as-a-Judge)

sub_skills.skill_content: LLM-as-judge uses a model to score another model's outputs against criteria, such as accuracy, tone or completeness. It scales to many outputs where human review would be slow. Judges can be biased, for example toward longer answers, so clear rubrics are needed and results should be checked against human ratings.

LLM as a Judge: Scaling AI Evaluation Strategies

sub_skills.skill_content: Regression testing reruns your eval set every time a prompt, model or context setup changes. It catches cases where a change that fixes one problem breaks something that used to work. Running it automatically on each change keeps quality from drifting without anyone noticing.

rsc.title: Automated Regression Testing: The Complete 2026 Guide
Watch the language: A tutorial on regression testing for LLMs - Evidently AI
Regression Testing for LLMs: Golden Datasets Explained

skills.skill_content: Context evaluation checks whether the information given to the model is good, separately from the prompt. For RAG systems this means asking whether retrieval found the right documents, and whether the answer is supported by them. Measuring these two parts separately shows whether a failure comes from retrieval or from generation.

rsc.title: 4 RAG Metrics to Improve Retrieval and Generation
AI Agent Context Evaluation: How to Test a Context Change
AI Agent Evaluation - Machine Learning Mastery
RAGAS: How to Evaluate a RAG Application

skills.skill_content: Prompt management is how a team stores, versions, reviews and monitors the prompts used in a product. Prompts are treated like code: they have owners, history and tests. This makes changes safe and easy to roll back, and shows how a prompt performs in production.

rsc.title: Prompt Management 101 - Full Guide for AI Engineers

sub_skills.skill_content: Prompt versioning means keeping a history of each prompt change, with the date, the reason and its evaluation results. When quality drops, you can compare versions and roll back. Recording what you tried and why also saves others from repeating failed experiments.

rsc.title: What is prompt versioning? Best practices for iteration without breaking production
What Is Prompt Versioning? A Complete Guide for Engineering Teams in 2026

sub_skills.skill_content: Context isolation gives each sub-task or sub-agent its own separate context. A sub-agent does a focused job, such as searching or reviewing, and returns only a short result to the main agent. This keeps noise and mistakes from spreading and keeps the main context small.

rsc.title: Building Reliable AI Agents with Sub-Agent Context Isolation in Claude Code

sub_skills.skill_content: In multi-agent systems, context sharing decides what information passes between agents. Sharing too little leaves an agent without what it needs, while sharing too much brings back the clutter that isolation was meant to remove. Common approaches are passing short summaries or structured results, using shared memory or files, and giving each agent only the parts relevant to its job.

rsc.title: Context Management for Multi-Agent Systems: Context Patterns
How to Implement Multi-Agent Context Sharing Patterns - Fast.io
Multi Agent Systems Explained: How AI Agents & LLMs Work Together
A2A vs MCP: AI Agent Communication Explained

skills.skill_content: Inference engineering is the practice of making generative AI models faster, less expensive, and more reliable to serve in production. It spans the full stack from CUDA kernels and GPU architecture to Kubernetes autoscaling and multi-cloud capacity management. The field emerged alongside the explosion of open models and the shift from pay-per-token APIs to dedicated deployments, where engineers own latency, throughput, cost, and uptime directly.

rsc.title: What Is Inference Engineering? The 2026 GPU Cloud Guide
A Guide to AI Inference Engineering
AI Inference: The Secret to AI's Superpowers

sub_skills.skill_content: Closed models are accessed exclusively through a vendor API; the weights are never released. Open models publish their weights for download and self-hosting. For inference engineers, this distinction determines the entire problem space: closed models require no infrastructure but offer no control over latency, cost, or configuration, while open models require building and operating a full inference stack but give complete control over every layer of it.

rsc.title: AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models
Open-source Models vs. Closed-Source Models: A Simple Guide
Open-Source vs. Closed LLMs: A Guide
Open Source vs Closed AI: LLMs, Agents & the AI Stack Explained

sub_skills.skill_content: Training is the process of learning model weights from data. Inference is serving those weights in production to generate outputs. Training runs are compute-intensive batch jobs; inference is a continuous, latency-sensitive service. Where training success is measured in loss curves, inference success is measured in time to first token, tokens per second, and uptime.

Shared inference means sending requests to a public API and paying per token. Dedicated inference means renting GPUs and running your own model server, paying per GPU-hour. Shared inference is simpler and has no cold start, but dedicated inference offers control over latency, cost at scale, model customization, and uptime. Most products start shared and move to dedicated as traffic grows.

rsc.title: Dedicated vs shared LLM inference: when reserved capacity makes sense
Self-Hosted LLM: A Practical Guide for DevOps
When shared inference is not enough: the case for dedicated AI endpoints

sub_skills.skill_content: A complete inference system has three layers: runtime, infrastructure, and tooling. The runtime layer optimizes a single model on a single instance using techniques like batching, caching, quantization, and speculation. The infrastructure layer scales across clusters, regions, and cloud providers while maintaining uptime. The tooling layer provides the right level of abstraction for engineers to control the system productively. All three must work together for mission-critical inference at scale.

rsc.title: The Inference Stack
rsc.content: A complete inference system has three layers: runtime, infrastructure, and tooling. The runtime layer optimizes a single model on a single instance using techniques like batching, caching, quantization, and speculation. The infrastructure layer scales across clusters, regions, and cloud providers while maintaining uptime. The tooling layer provides the right level of abstraction for engineers to control the system productively. All three must work together for mission-critical inference at scale.

sub_skills.skill_content: TTFT measures how long it takes for a user to receive the first output token after submitting a request. It is determined primarily by the prefill phase and by queue time. For streaming applications like chatbots, TTFT is the most visible latency signal and directly affects perceived responsiveness.

rsc.title: What is time to first token (TTFT)?
What Is Time to First Token?
Most devs don't understand how LLM tokens work

sub_skills.skill_content: TPS measures how many tokens are delivered to the user per second after the first token. It is determined by the decode phase and reflects memory bandwidth efficiency. Per-user TPS (also called perceived TPS) is a latency metric; total TPS across the inference service is a throughput metric.

rsc.title: LLM Speed Tiers Explained: What TPS (Token Per Second) Actually Feels Like

sub_skills.skill_content: ITL is the time between successive generated tokens during decode. An ITL of 10 milliseconds corresponds to 100 tokens per second. It is the per-step measure underlying TPS and is directly tied to how quickly the GPU can complete a single decode forward pass.

Lower latency means faster responses per user; higher throughput means more total requests served per unit time. These goals are often in tension. Increasing batch size improves throughput but worsens per-user latency. Choosing the right balance is one of the primary decisions in configuring an inference service.

rsc.title: The LLM Inference Trilemma: Throughput, Latency, Cost
LLM inference latency: TTFT, tokens per second, and what to measure
⚖️ Latency vs Throughput: Deep Dive into System Performance Trade‑Offs

sub_skills.skill_content: Mean latency hides outliers. LLM response times follow a right-skewed distribution, so engineers measure P50, P90, P95, and P99. A P99 of several seconds means one in a hundred users has a poor experience even if the median is fast. Reducing P90/P99 latency is as important as reducing average latency.

rsc.title: Percentiles vs averages: why your latency dashboard lies
Latency percentiles for load testing analysis
Mastering Latency Metrics: P90, P95, P99 | System Design

sub_skills.skill_content: End-to-end latency includes inference time, network round-trip, queue time, and client-side overhead. Inference-only metrics tell you how well the model server performs; end-to-end metrics tell you what users actually experience. When inference time is fast but end-to-end time is slow, the bottleneck is in infrastructure or client code, not the GPU.

rsc.title: 10 LLM Inference Metrics Every AI Engineer Must Know
9 Key LLM Inference Metrics Explained in 5 Minutes

sub_skills.skill_content: RTF measures how quickly an ASR system can process audio relative to its duration. A system that transcribes one hour of audio in six seconds has an RTF of 600x. It is the standard throughput metric for long-file transcription workloads and improves roughly linearly with the number of GPUs used for parallel chunk processing.

rsc.title: What is RTF (Real-Time Factor) in ASR?    Copied from: https://www.futurebeeai.com/knowledge-hub/real-time-factor-asr

skills.skill_content: A neural network is a layered structure of nodes where each node applies a learned weight matrix and bias to its input. Multiple layers connected in sequence form the foundation for all generative AI models. Inference engineers need a working model of how neural networks compute outputs to understand where performance bottlenecks arise.

rsc.title: But what is a neural network?

sub_skills.skill_content: Neural networks can be organized as encoder-only, decoder-only, or encoder-decoder models. Modern LLMs are decoder-only. Encoder-only models like BERT are used for text embeddings and classification. Encoder-decoder models like Whisper use an encoder to process input into an internal representation and a decoder to generate output tokens autoregressively. Each architecture has different inference characteristics and tooling requirements.

skills.skill_content: An LLM is a decoder-only transformer with three main components: an embedding layer that converts input tokens to vectors, a stack of transformer blocks that process those vectors, and an output language modeling head that converts the final hidden states into a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The configuration file for an open model specifies all architectural details including layer count, hidden dimensions, and attention heads.

rsc.title: Build a Large Language Model From Scratch
What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?

sub_skills.skill_content: Transformer blocks are the repeated hidden layers of an LLM. Each block contains an attention sublayer, a feed-forward neural network sublayer, and normalization layers. The feed-forward network holds the majority of model parameters, while attention is the most computationally complex operation per token.

rsc.title: What Are Transformer Models and How Do They Work?
A Simplified Explanation of the Transformer Block

sub_skills.skill_content: Attention is the mechanism transformers use to relate each token to all previous tokens via query, key, and value projections. During decode, each new token attends to every prior token, and the KV cache stores precomputed keys and values to avoid recomputation. Attention is the most expensive and most heavily optimized operation in LLM inference.

The KV cache stores the key and value tensors computed during attention for each previously processed token. Without it, attention would require recomputing every prior token on each decode step, making inference prohibitively slow. The KV cache lives in GPU memory and its size grows with sequence length and batch size, making it a major target for memory management techniques.

rsc.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
KV Caching Explained: Optimizing Transformer Inference Efficiency
How KV Cache Speeds Up LLMs for Faster AI Models on GPUs
The KV Cache: Memory Usage in Transformers

sub_skills.skill_content: Mixture of Experts models replace dense linear layers with a set of smaller expert matrices, activating only a subset of experts per token via a learned router. A model like Qwen3-235B activates only 22 billion of its 235 billion parameters per forward pass, making single-user inference efficient. In batched production serving, different tokens activate different experts, so nearly all parameters are active across the batch.

rsc.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
A Visual Guide to Mixture of Experts (MoE) in LLMs

sub_skills.skill_content: LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input sequence in parallel to build the KV cache and is compute-bound. Decode generates output tokens one at a time by reading model weights from memory and is memory-bound. Each phase has different bottlenecks and responds to different optimization techniques.

rsc.title: Prefill vs Decode: LLM Inference Phases Explained
Understanding the Two Key Stages of LLM Inference: Prefill and Decode(Part-1)
Why LLMs Read Fast but Write Slowly - Prefill vs Decode

sub_skills.skill_content: Online inference serves real-time user-facing requests where latency matters. Offline inference processes large batches of data asynchronously where throughput and cost matter more than per-request speed. The same model, like Whisper for transcription, may need separate deployments for each use case because the optimal configurations differ significantly.

rsc.title: Production ML systems: Static versus dynamic inference
Trade-offs in Online vs Offline Model Inference
Offline Recurrence for Improved Online Inference

sub_skills.skill_content: Asynchronous inference is a fire-and-forget request model where the client submits a job, receives an immediate acknowledgment, and retrieves the result later via a webhook. It is suited for throughput-sensitive, latency-insensitive workloads like bulk document embedding or corpus transcription. Async jobs have much longer time limits than synchronous requests and require robust server-side queuing.

AI-native applications are products where generative models power the core user experience, from code editors and voice agents to customer support and media generation. Each category has different inference requirements. Agents generate many inference calls per user action; chat applications prioritize TTFT; voice applications need low end-to-end latency for natural conversation.

sub_skills.skill_content: Consumer applications are cost-sensitive and have unpredictable traffic spikes, requiring flexible autoscaling and low marginal cost. Business-to-business applications prioritize uptime and consistent low latency, as they often sit in the critical path of revenue-generating workflows. Compliance requirements, including data residency and regulatory certifications, are more common in enterprise deployments.

Reasoning models generate an intermediate thinking sequence before producing their final output, adding a third token sequence alongside the input and output. This reasoning trace increases total token count significantly and changes inference economics: TTFT is higher, total latency is longer, and output token costs dominate. Inference engineers must account for the variable and sometimes very long reasoning sequences when sizing infrastructure and setting latency budgets.

skills.skill_content: Image and video models are specialized artificial intelligence architectures designed to process, interpret, and generate visual data. These models utilize techniques like convolutional neural networks (CNNs), transformers, and diffusion processes to analyze pixel patterns for tasks such as object detection, image classification, and video frame synthesis.
